utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any leftovers that were announced are not necessarily to be dealt with before we have concluded the testimony of the witness. Therefore, the Chamber suggests that we leave them until after we've concluded the hearing of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both is okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Ms. Hasan will now continue her cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. No. Any questions, Mr. Lukic? Mr. Stojanovic? It's really time for a holiday because ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have just a few questions, as we indicated yesterday, and I would now like to ask Mr. Kovacevic those questions with your kind permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, I would now like to go through the time line of events on the 12th of July, as far as you're able to remember, of course. In your statement, in paragraph 14, you said that you received the order to head towards Potocari sometime between 1000 and 1100 hours; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you: To the best of your recollection, when did you reach Potocari, approximately? When did you reach the area where you indicated yesterday that you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around noon, half past 12.00, not later than 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next step, to the best of your recollection, how much time did you spend in that area, on the road in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the building itself, after the interview, hmm, I may have spent not more than 7 to 8 minutes. This is when the general came. And then we moved behind the building and we spent about half an hour there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next step, you receive further orders to go back to your initial positions, and now, to the best of your recollection, when did you leave the area of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at 1.30, not later than that. After we received the order we left the area where the houses were. There is a road behind the Cinkara, the factory. We crossed the bridge and then we went back to the Djogazi-Peciste line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how many people, how many soldiers, were there escorting General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't give you the exact number but I think about five or six people. Not more than that. But I didn't really look all that closely. After the General addressed us and told us to move on, we simply left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that time, did you notice at any time that General Mladic addressed the people there, using a loud speaker?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We went to the other side, and we did not see what happened with the General because he was on the other side. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the person that might be your neighbour or your -- or the neighbour of the woman that -- whose statement you heard yesterday, whose name is Momir, who was supposed to be in your unit that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Momir was not with me. I only know Momir, aka Penzijica, who was the deputy commander for security, and I think that we had not seen each other for a month before those events, and I don't even recall if we met at all after the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I would like us to look at the document that has the 65 ter number 31004 and let us look at page 2 of this document in the B/C/S version, and I think it's page 2 in the English version as well. I would like to look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, look at the last paragraph in B/C/S. It is the penultimate passage on this page in the English version, Your Honours. It says here in the statement taken from this witness: The next morning, Ratko Mladic arrived. Would this correspond to the time when you were in Potocari, this statement made by this witness that it was in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all of my statements, I said that around 10.00 a.m., I received an order, while I was at the initial positions. After that we had to prepare the unit, we had to gather up, and then we had to move from the top of Caus to Potocari. In normal conditions, regular conditions, if you don't search the terrain, it would take you an hour to get there. So this -- I don't know, really, what to say. I don't see how this could be true. Also, several thousand people? Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will be asking you about that specifically in a minute. So the next part of this sentence reads, okay: "Ratko Mladic arrived with several thousand of his soldiers." Were you able to estimate now, not counting these people who were escorting General Mladic, as you told us, how many people -- how many soldiers of the VRS could have been there, counting your soldiers too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My soldiers were in the courtyard of this building. They were not out in the street. The general showed up, he was walking from Srebrenica, and on both sides of the road there was this huge crowd of people from Srebrenica, women, children and so on. I noticed the general as he approached. Before that, or indeed afterwards as I was on my way back, I did not see any troops, apart from those people that I saw while we were behind this building. So a hundred soldiers, it's a huge mass of people. You would have to notice them. The general showed up, he was on foot, and he was surrounded by five, six, a maximum of eight people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like us to move on to the next page in the B/C/S version, the English version is fine. I would like us to focus on the last paragraph on this page in the English version, Your Honours. It says in this statement: "With my neighbour Momir and Zoran Kovacevic, son of Bosko, born in the village of Hurenovac," well, it says "Hurenovac" here, "Bratunac municipality."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Kunjerac, it's a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. So is there a village in the Srebrenica municipality that would have something to do with your life, which would be called Hurenovac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of your village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Kunjerac. It's called Kunjerac. A hamlet of the village of Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me finish by asking you if, at any time after the war, on any occasion, in any situation, you have been able to meet with the witness who provided this statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. And since I hunt, I walk around her house, as I go out to hunt, and her neighbours sometimes ask me to help them, if they have something to be done. I have heard that she lives in Srebrenica but I can't verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After the war, have you at any time, Mr. Kovacevic, have any personal problems with your Muslim neighbours who have come back?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. We are on the same terms as we used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of terms are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were friends, neighbours. There is no difference that would be based on ethnicity, at least that's the way I feel about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have those people returned to their homes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are mostly poor people. They had nowhere to go. I think that at least the elderly have come back. There are some young people, but I don't know them, really, so I can't tell you who they are, but for the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, thank you very much for your clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Judge Fluegge has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, Mr. Stojanovic asked you a minute ago what is the name of your village. You said: "It's called Kunjerac, a hamlet of the village of Loznica." Is that the place where you lived in -- used to live in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's where my father and my family live. I live in Bratunac. I have a house in the Podgradac neighbourhood of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is Loznica a part of the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were born there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you still living in -- it's not recorded. You said: "I have a house in the ... neighbourhood of Bratunac." But can you please repeat the name of the location.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Podgradac. It's about 1200 metres from the centre of Bratunac in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you used to live there in 1995 and also today; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I moved into my house in 1980 and I have been living there, it's my own house, since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you're still living there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, could you think of any reason why Ms. Salihovic would lie about what she stated specifically as far as your activities are concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have given this some thought, when my father told me that she had said that, so I have been thinking about it since then and I really cannot think of a reason why. Perhaps if she saw the interview, she may have been prompted by something to say that, but now as to what this motive was, I really can't think of it, because if it had happened the way she described it, it would be only logical for her to tell me, to ask me: Neighbour, were you there or not? Or if she realised that she had made a mistake, now it would be only natural for her to apologise to me because of course, you can make a mistake, but if you realise that you've made a mistake, you have to do something about it. I really cannot comprehend why she has done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say that you expected her to ask you whether you were there or to apologise if she made a mistake. If she is quite positive in her recollection, there would be no need to ask you. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but she could at least come to me and say: "Why did you do it," out of resentment, because if I were in her shoes, that's what I would do. I would ask her: "Why did you do that?" Because if there is somebody who did something bad, you can't keep on being friends with them. My brother was killed in 1992. If I had heard that somebody had killed him, I would not feel resentment but I would ask this person: "Why did you kill my brother?" So I really -- if you think about this in purely human terms, as a human being, I really cannot understand it. In particular, the fact that she established this link between me and Momir, and the war ended 20 years ago. People know everything in Bratunac and I have never heard anyone in Bratunac say that somebody from Bratunac took part in the separation, apart from Momir, aka Penzijica. We all know what happened, and the moment General Mladic appeared, everybody was running away from him, like the devil from the cross, and that's what we did. And now she is saying this. I could understand it if I had been close to the factory but I was not. So there was no possibility for her to see me at all. There was just this interview, this footage. Maybe that's what prompted her to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever try to find out who separated families at that point in time? Because if you say you are accused of having participated, did you ever try to find out who, then, if not you, did such things?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody in Bratunac, everybody is saying things about that. It's being discussed because it's a matter of general interest. Of course, I am ready to be held accountable for everything that I have done and I'm a reserve officer, I know what my responsibilities are. I am ready to be held accountable for the things that I did, but this is something that I did not do and that's why I'm bothered by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not really an answer to my question. My question was whether you ever tried to find out who, then, may have separated members of families at that point in time, at that location.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you talk to people in Bratunac, you know who is supposed to know things. It's not the people who were in the army but those who were milling about. And I'm always trying to find out, I have been trying to find out, who took part in the separation, and I have not heard from anyone about anyone else because people from our brigade were there. Perhaps some civilian from Bratunac took part in that, but whoever I talk to, they were unable to identify any other person that took part in it. Somebody that I could talk to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said it was not members of the army? Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. I'm saying members of the army, members of civilian structures from Bratunac, because it would have to be that the army or the civilian structures, as I've said. And through all these conversations, had I ever been told a single name of any person, either from the army or from the civilian structures, I would have said so. I would have cleared my own name, if you will. But really, nobody in Bratunac could have told me anything, whoever I talked to. It's been 15 years or so. And then people say they heard this or that or saw this and that, but this directly, because I'm interested in that too, I simply don't know. Perhaps someday there will be proceedings regarding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're saying, members of the civilian structures, who do you have in mind, or who were perhaps talked about as members of the civilian structures being there at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that people were talking, but I'm just assuming that in those moments, it is only the civilian structures of government that can decide and the army and the SUP. There is nobody else. That's why I'm saying it's either the civilian structures or the army or the MUP. Who else could it have been? It's not that someone can come in as a private individual and do that kind of thing. So it's either in the name of the army or of the civilian authorities or of the SUP. That is something I never managed to find out. The only truth I know is Momir, Penzijica. He's the only one who was there, he knows who he operated with, and I really don't know anything about that. I really wouldn't talk about that because I could only engage in guesswork and that wouldn't be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this Momir, Penzijica, who was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic, nicknamed Penzijica, that's what we call him. We often forget his real name. The deputy commander of the brigade, the deputy chief of security of the brigade actually, and he has been convicted and he said everything he had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you did not talk to him in person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I had no opportunity to do that. Before Srebrenica, a month before that, I think I did not see him, and I never saw him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. You said you didn't see General Mladic addressing the crowd by megaphone. Did you hear anything? Because the use of a megaphone may carry quite a distance.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't interested. To tell you the truth, I wasn't even paying attention. I don't remember. My memory doesn't tell me anything. This really has not remained in my memory. About 50 metres behind that building or so, that's where we were, by some other houses so why would I say anything else? I can only say what is true, and that is that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Ms. Hasan, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, just a few, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, do you realise that Ms. Salihovic provided her statement on the 26th of July, 1995, shortly after these events?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. And it was provided to the -- to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't know. I really don't know. This is the first time I see this here. I heard from my old father that that's what she said, and if you look at the statement, you can probably see the date and everything. But I really did not know about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that Momir is a fairly common name in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in our area, but here she says her neighbour Momir and I. Momir, Penzijica, in Bratunac, well, he's two kilometres towards Kravica, Bjelovac -- actually Biljaca, where she is, is seven kilometres along the Drina River, so that is ten kilometres between Momir's house and his -- and her house. And mine, sort of. So Momir, Penzijica, cannot be her neighbour and mine. And then there are Muslims there, and then Kovacevic and Stojanovic, my family. So her neighbour, Momir? No way. This can only relate to Momir, Penzijica, as far as I can see, but to say that he is her neighbour or mine, that would not be right. It's a lot, ten kilometres. That's not a neighbour, a person who lives ten kilometres away. And then also Momir was a high school teacher. If she went to the high school in Bratunac where Momir taught, then she could have known him as a teacher from there. So, really, this linking of me and Momir, saying that we are neighbours, it just isn't right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, for one thing, she does not mention Momir's last name, nor does she mention his nickname Penzijica. This is something you have told us. You have created this link. And we know that Momir Nikolic has admitted about being involved in the separation of able-bodied men in Potocari, and Ms. Salihovic here points out that a Momir was there with you. So it is you today who draws the link between you and Momir and, in fact, it's because you were there with Momir Nikolic separating these men. Is that not the case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just as if you'd say that you and I were in Potocari. It would be equally true. So this has nothing to do with it. She is speaking about Momir and the only Momir I know as Momir is that one. I don't know anyone else. I did not have a single soldier by the name of Momir. Also, in my village, in all of Loznica, that is several hamlets, I don't think there is a single Momir to this day. I really don't know who this Momir could be. The only Momir I know is that one and not a single other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Kovacevic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties and put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again. And you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first ask the parties whether they have any matters to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These were sent by e-mail. Just to put them on the record, it relates to MFI D553. The Prosecution has discussed the tendering of a still image from the video from which excerpts MFI D553 were taken and have agreed, as far as I understand, about the tendering of still image from 06 seconds, at 06 seconds of the full video which is -- the still image has been uploaded under 65 ter 31013. Now, the parties as I understand, agree that Sedrenik appears in the foreground and that the ridge of -- I'm going to mispronounce this, Spicasta Stijena is also visible in the image. So basically the Prosecution is seeking to admit 65 ter 31013 and understands that there is no objection to that, and also does not object to the admission of D553.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. That has been agreed. So if you just allow me one more sentence now that I'm on my feet. D248, according to the information I have, has remained pending and I would like to inform the Trial Chamber, I'd like it to be on the record, that after we discussed this with the Prosecution, we are prepared to inform the Trial Chamber that we give up on tendering this document, D248.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, D248 is vacated. D553 is admitted into evidence. And would you please assign a number to the still of D553 which is uploaded under number 31013.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31013 receives number D595, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D559 is admitted -- I misspoke, D595 is admitted into evidence. Any further matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just to inform the Chamber that we confirm that the protective measures for Witness GRM277 are to be the same as those provided in the Kunarac case and that's pseudonym and face distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They continue to apply.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And then in relation to GRM311, the Prosecution has reviewed the testimony of that witness in the D Milosevic case and has decided that it will not make any further submissions in that regard. And it won't be tendering additional portions of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. This may overlap, I'm not quite certain about that, with a matter I would raise later. Could I first deal with the following matter. It's about disclosure. On the 15th of July of this year, the Prosecution has expressed concerns about the Defence not being able to meet its disclosure obligation pursuant to the agreement between the parties. The agreement of the 15th of May sets out, inter alia, that the Defence agrees to disclose witness statements which have not already been disclosed pursuant to the agreement as soon as practicable, and in any case no later than the 15th of August. The Prosecution suggested that the Chamber requests a detailed report from the Defence as to the status of disclosure and weekly reports from the Defence until the disclosure is complete. The Chamber is not inclined to follow the proposal by the Prosecution but strongly urges the Defence to inform the Prosecution and the Chamber, without delay, if there is a problem meeting the deadline agreed on by the parties. I would like to briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I have a few matters in relation to the testimony of Luka Dragicevic, which we heard on the 8th and the 9th of July. On the 9th of July, during the cross-examination of Luka Dragicevic, the Prosecution relied upon P6648, which is a Serbian State Security Service note dated the 2nd of November, 1992. The Prosecution tendered the document under seal. The Defence objected, as it was a statement of a third-party witness not present in court to attest to it. The Chamber made a remark that there was a distinction between different kinds of statements and the attestation of a statement by a third-party witness should occur if that statement has been taken for the purposes of proceedings before the Tribunal. The Chamber then asked the Defence if the Judges had previously stated otherwise during the Prosecution case, and if so, when. The Defence sought time to review the trial transcript and refer to the Chamber. The Chamber is seeking a follow-up on this issue with the Defence, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we gave a transcript reference in court that day. I dealt with the witness and I believe there was a transcript reference to a protected witness - we are in open session - and I believe that reference is given in court following the break, following one of the breaks in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will check whether that is a -- I have a vague recollection that we looked at that and that the situation was quite different but I'm not sure about it. So therefore we will verify it and if the situation is indeed very different, we will let you know through an informal communication and in that case would invite you again to give further references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you have any recollection exactly, apart from that it was after the break, but any page, any date, any line, so that we can perhaps check it even during the break and -- if you would try, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to retrace our steps on the transcript, if I can. I can't remember the exact -- actually, I do now remember the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, we'll have a look at it during the break, if you do the same, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move on. On the 9th of July, during the cross-examination of Luka Dragicevic, the Prosecution relied upon the following exhibits: P6649, which was a criminal report dated the 26th of October, 1992; P6650, a receipt dated the 28th of September, 1992, for weapons received by Milan Lukic from the VRS Visegrad command; and lastly, P6651, which was a certificate issued by the 1st Visegrad Infantry Brigade. P6649 was tendered by the Prosecution under seal. All three of these exhibits were MFI'd pending provision of provenance information by the Prosecution, and the Chamber would like to receive that provenance information. If you do not have it immediately available, we would hear from you after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take the break first. There are a few matters the parties have to sort out during that break. The Chamber will then give the guidance it announced and we also may spend a word on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic or Mr. Lukic, my colleague draws my attention to the fact that when I read the issue about the disclosure, report on disclosure, which we were inclined not to do but then urged the Defence to inform the Prosecution, the Chamber, without delay, if there would be a problem meeting the deadline agreed on by the parties, that you were on your feet and I may have missed that. I don't know if you want to add anything or make any submissions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that from that moment the situation changed drastically. We started actually to send the statements. I was not aware that our case manager is not forwarding the statements to the Prosecution. So I think that the situation changed, and I don't see any major problems in meeting our deadline by the 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that would change in any way, then we would like to be informed immediately and you should give notice to the Defence -- to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having dealt with all that, we take a break first, and we will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00, then hear a few matters from the parties, and the Chamber will issue the guidance and will also say something about the restart after the recess. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were a few leftovers from before the break. Mr. Ivetic, could you -- did you find the reference to where you responded to the issue that was raised about admissibility of statements taken by third parties, not for Tribunal purposes, and their admissibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The discussion was at transcript page 23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you give me one second, then I'll try to immediately look at it. Was that the 9th of July or was it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look. 9th of July. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Transcript page 23752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, 752. I'm with you on 752.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And therein, I talked about a statement taken by the Bosnian AID, 1D1370, that was discussed at transcript pages 18.000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, let me just first find your reference. Line 5, I hear. "Just while we are waiting, Your Honours, I can direct Your Honours to transcript page 18652 through 18654." Yes, I have a vague recollection that we looked at it at the time but let's do it again at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And then there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was 18 -- and that's -- let's have a look. Let me see what date that is, 18652. 652 that should be the 1st of November. Yes. Yes. I'm at 18652. And where, then, exactly we said because it's -- could you assist us, Mr. Ivetic, what exactly was said there which would support --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: THE admission of the AID statement 1D1370 was denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was denied. And for what reason exactly and where do we find that? Mr. Shin said: "This is not the proper way of introducing a witness, particularly one that the Defence intends to call as Mr. Lukic indicated." Then I asked Mr. Lukic to respond specifically on it, and then there was an issue about relevance. And then I said: "If you want to call that person as a witness, then you are, of course, free to do so, if there will be a Defence case, Mr. Lukic." And we denied the admission, but where do I read, because that was the crucial point, where do I read that it was because it was a statement taken by a third party. Because here there is certainly a -- I remember that we looked at it at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- upon you giving this reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We did, and then we had a further discussion at transcript page 23765 on the matter, again on the 9th of July, where we went through this. And you had asked if it's different where a witness is on the Defence witness list, and I indicated that at the time that the admission of that document was denied, there was no Defence witness list in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but it was announced that he would be called as a Defence witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so even if there is no formal list. But where do I see, because that was the issue, that just because it was a statement taken by a third party, that that would make that statement inadmissible? Because that is the issue that was your claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was my objection, and you asked for one reference and we gave this reference which we believe, that's how we understood the denial of admission to be based upon the fact that it's a statement of an out-of-court declarant that we [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, under those very specific circumstances. Isn't it true that we have admitted many, many statements which were taken out of court by third parties, not taken for the purposes of this Tribunal, and that if there was not such a -- such a complicating factor, that we usually just admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's not my recollection. It's not the recollection of my colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we -- I do then understand that -- and did I -- you said it was again discussed at --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 23765, where you raised the issue of it being a Defence witness and we talked about the same things that we just talked about now. So we talked about it twice on the 9th of July, this particular transcript selection from the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just reread it. I think it starts at 23765 almost at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph -- page -- line 18. So then in all clarity, what the Chamber would like to receive from you is a reference in which clearly and, if not exclusively, then at least mainly on the basis that a statement was taken not for Tribunal -- that a statement was taken by a third party although not for Tribunal purposes, that that in itself was a reason to deny admission. I think that's what the Chamber is seeking at this moment. If you could find one, we would appreciate if would you bring it to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will endeavour to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Then what else do we have? I think the provenance of 6649, 6650, and 6651 were -- and these numbers relate to P exhibits that we are -- still would like receive that from the Prosecution. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. With respect to P6649, that's the official criminal report from the Uzice SUP regarding the detention of Milan Lukic dated 28 October 1992. The Prosecution received that document from the Republic of Serbia pursuant to RFA SRB 1696 which requested the criminal case file from the district court of Uzice against those same proceedings against Milan Lukic for the possession of illegal arms in October 1992. According to these materials, the charges were dismissed on 4 November 1992. With respect to the P6650, these were two certificates that were issued by the Visegrad command of the VRS confirming the issuance of weapons and communication radio to Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could you please slow down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We noticed that it would be very difficult for the interpreters. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you to everyone. This was also received pursuant to RFA SRB 1696, so the same criminal case file. P6651 are the certificates issued by the 1st Visegrad Infantry Brigade related to Milan Lukic's and Dragan Dragicevic's membership in the brigade. The ERN that was tendered for this document is 04224603. With respect to this document we got from an individual source, the document also is identical to ERNs 06446129 and 06446130 in the Prosecution's possession, which also originate from the criminal case file related to the same criminal proceedings from the Uzice court. We received a copy of the same versions of these certificates pursuant to RFA SRB 1696. With respect to the document P6651, it was previously admitted as Exhibit P314 on 26 March 2009 in the case of Prosecutor versus Lukic. This can be found at transcript page 6375 of the Lukic proceedings. That's the information available to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do the objections stand against admission? I think it was not objections but it was just pending further information about provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's my recollection as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now having received that information, is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6649, P6650, and P6651, which were marked for identification, are hereby admitted into evidence. I think we have dealt with all the leftovers from before the break. Any other matter to be raised by the parties? Then I would finally give the guidance the Chamber announced. The Chamber has carefully considered the use of court time from the beginning of the Defence case until this point in the proceeding and notes that in several respects the parties should improve. The Chamber recalls the frequent guidance it gave during the Prosecution's case in chief to which it now adds the following guidance. At the outset, the Chamber notes its responsibility for ensuring the rights of the accused as set forth in the Statute but emphasises that this duty must be exercised with the -- and at the same time the Chamber should meet its obligation to ensure an expeditious trial. To this end, the Chamber notes with concern that many court hours have been spent adducing evidence of questionable relevance, much of which appears at this moment to also have questionable probative value. Many Defence witnesses have given a great deal of evidence about matters that neither appear to form part of any recognisable defence, nor relate in any material way to the crimes alleged in the indictment. Additionally, during cross-examination, it has often come to light that the source of a witness's knowledge about a particular incident merely stems from media reports or from the Karadzic Defence. The Chamber also notes that often these witnesses make sweeping generalisations in their statements which then trigger the Prosecution to spend a great amount of time in cross-examination attempting to show what is readily apparent from the start; that is, that sweeping generalisations have little, if any, probative value. Conversely, relevant content has sometimes been removed from witness statements, apparently triggering the Prosecution's need to explore these subjects as well as the reasons for removing them, all of which needlessly uses a great deal of valuable court time. Moreover, the Chamber notes the unfortunate tendency of both parties to adduce evidence that is unnecessarily repetitious or that relates to matters that are not in dispute in the first place. For example, the Chamber has now heard several witnesses give evidence concerning the strength and positions of ABiH units, but when these matters are explored by the Chamber in court, it discovers that the parties are more or less in agreement about such facts and there was never a reason to spend court time adducing the evidence to begin with. Lastly, the Chamber notes the frequency with which the Defence has been ill prepared to present evidence in the form of witness statements. There have been numerous occasions in which different versions of a witness statement have been mixed up. The statement tendered in the Rule 92 ter motion has turned out to be different from the version offered in court, the wrong documents have been uploaded into e-court, and documents have been misidentified in Defence Exhibit lists. More significantly, the Chamber notes with serious concern that witnesses have testified about alarming statement-taking practices, such as being pressured to sign statements which they knew to contain errors, or signing statements that they have not read. A great deal of court time has been used trying to clarify and correct such issues as, for example, those encountered with the statements of Witnesses Deronjic, Batinic, and Tusevljak. For the reasons discussed, and in keeping with its responsibility to conduct an efficient and expeditious trial, the Chamber finds it necessary to issue the following guidance to the parties which the Chamber expects to be followed closely for the remainder of the trial. First, the parties are expected to limit the production of evidence to matters that are relevant and start by adducing evidence which is most relevant. The Chamber reminds the parties that relevant evidence has been defined by the Appeals Chamber as evidence relating to a material issue and that the material issues of a case are to be found in the indictment. Inasmuch as the Defence finds it's preferable to use witness statements from other trials, it is expected to remove irrelevant material from such statements before they are tendered in this case. Similarly, the Prosecution is expected to not waste court time cross-examining witnesses on matters of questionable relevance. Second, the Chamber expects each party to pay close attention to the probative value of the evidence it adduces or seeks to counter. In short, this means that the Defence should avoid adducing evidence, including in written statements, for which there is no factual basis or which could be characterised as a sweeping generalisation. Similarly, the Prosecution should carefully consider how much time, if any, is needed to test such unsubstantiated evidence on cross-examination. The Chamber draws the attention of the parties to its 3rd of July, 2012, decision on the admission of exhibits tendered through Witness Harland, in which the Chamber stated that, absent corroborating evidence, weight will not be given to the unsupported, unsourced opinion of a witness. Third, the Chamber expects the parties to carefully consider the necessity of adducing repetitious or background evidence. The Chamber reminds the Defence that should it wish to offer evidence that is, for example, cumulative in nature, or which relates to the historical, political, or military background of the case, it should seek to do so pursuant to Rule 92 bis, a Rule created precisely for the purpose of expediting complex trials by eliminating the need to use court time for adducing such evidence. The Prosecution is similarly urged to carefully consider what, if any, cross-examination is needed when presented with such background evidence. Fourth, the Chamber expects the parties to work together to avoid adducing evidence about matters which are not in dispute. This cannot be over-emphasised. There should be a question asked by each party before any statement is tendered or any question is put to a witness: Does this concern a matter that is in dispute? If there is any doubt about the answer to this question for either party, the parties should work together on the matter rather than wasting valuable court time arguing about matters for which no argument is needed. Fifth, the Chamber expects the Defence to be significantly more diligent in the preparation and presentation of its case, especially with respect to the manner in which it obtains, corrects, and uses witness statements. To this end, the Chamber invites the Defence to seriously consider whether presenting its witnesses viva voce might be more conducive to an expeditious trial by avoiding arduous examinations concerning witness statements. In conclusion, the Chamber expects the parties to take seriously the guidance just delivered and make the changes necessary to follow it strictly. Otherwise, the Chamber will find itself in a position where it has to take action, such as denying the admission of evidence, including 92 ter statements, requiring 92 ter witnesses to testify viva voce, and terminating examinations of -- or cross-examinations due to lack of relevance or probative value. The Chamber now addresses the Defence in particular. The Chamber has been reluctant to consider the application of Rule 46 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence until this week, when the Chamber has again heard evidence of serious problems with the statement-taking practices of the Defence team. Should such questionable practices continue, the Chamber will be compelled to carefully consider whether and to what extent action might be necessary under Rule 46. And this concludes the guidance of the Chamber. The only matter now remaining is to adjourn. If the Chamber looks at the court calendar as it was issued until now, it seems that we would restart on the 26th of August, which is a Tuesday. The Chamber is not aware of any reason why we would not start on Monday, the 25th of August. Therefore, the parties should be prepared and the Chamber adjourns -- will adjourn until the 25th of August. If we have overlooked any reason which has caused the court calendar to tell us that it would be the 26th, then we will let you know as soon as possible. I do understand that Mr. Mladic would likely briefly consult, and since we are about to adjourn for the summer recess, you have an opportunity, if -- but at inaudible volume. At least for us inaudible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anything resulting from the consultations with Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's new topic. Mr. Mladic is complaining that he cannot continue sitting five days a week but it's really too tiresome for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That matter is pending and at this moment we are digesting the newest medical reports. And the Chamber will certainly consider whether those reports should have any consequences for the court schedule. So it's not that we are not continually thinking about it and it's not that we are not evaluating the newest report. One of the problems being that some of them were drafted in a language not everyone understands in this courtroom. Then we will adjourn and I wish everyone, although the Chamber is fully aware that circumstances are not the same for everyone, but I wish everyone a good time to have sufficient time to rest and to recover from the hard work everyone is doing in this courtroom, no one excluded. We adjourn and we will resume Monday, the 25th of August, 9.30 in the morning, courtroom -- most likely Courtroom I, but if any other courtroom, to be announced. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of August, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.
